--- title: "mimar: Compact Multiple Imputation, Assessment, and Reporting in R" subtitle: "Artificial amputation, chained-equations MI with ML imputers, diagnostic evaluation, and pooling, in one package" author: "Imad El Badisy" date: "2025-08-15" categories: [R, missing-data, packages] image: featured.png resources: featured.png execute: warning: false message: false --- Missing data is the rule, not the exception, in health research. Yet most workflows still string together three or four packages: one to characterize missingness, one to impute, one to pool, one to evaluate, with no consistent API across them. **mimar** brings all of that under one roof. ## What is mimar? `mimar` (v0.8.0) covers the full missing-data analysis cycle: 1. **Amputation**: artificially introduce missingness into a complete dataset for simulation studies 2. **Imputation**: single or multiple imputation via chained equations with a choice of statistical or ML imputers 3. **Evaluation**: diagnostic metrics comparing imputed distributions to observed and (when known) true values 4. **Pooling**: Rubin's rules applied to post-imputation model estimates Install: ```r install.packages("mimar") ``` ## Artificial amputation `ampute()` introduces controlled missingness into a complete data frame, specifying the mechanism (MCAR, MAR, MNAR) and the proportion of missing cells: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(mimar) set.seed(1) amp <- ampute(iris, prop = 0.25, mechanism = "MCAR") head(amp$data) # the amputed data frame ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # basetable: 6 x 5 Sepal.Length Sepal.Width Petal.Length Petal.Width Species 1 5.1 3.5 1.4 0.2 setosa 2 4.9 3.0 NA 0.2 setosa 3 4.7 3.2 1.3 0.2 4 4.6 3.1 1.5 NA setosa 5 NA 3.6 1.4 NA setosa 6 5.4 NA 1.7 0.4 setosa ``` ::: ::: ## Multiple imputation `impute()` runs chained equations with any registered imputer. The default is predictive mean matching (`"pmm"`), but ML-based imputers are equally accessible: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # PMM: the safe default imp_pmm <- impute(amp, m = 5, imputer = "pmm", maxit = 5) # Random forest imputation imp_rf <- impute(amp, m = 5, imputer = "ranger") # XGBoost imputation imp_xgb <- impute(amp, m = 5, imputer = "xgboost") class(imp_pmm) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "mimar_imputation" "list" ``` ::: ::: `impute()` returns a `mimar_imputation` object containing all `m` completed datasets alongside metadata for downstream steps. ## Available imputers ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} imputer_registry()[, c("imputer", "implementation", "stochastic")] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # basetable: 25 x 3 imputer implementation stochastic 1 mean mimar FALSE 2 median mimar FALSE 3 mode mimar FALSE 4 naive mimar FALSE 5 norm mimar TRUE 6 pmm mimar TRUE 7 spmm mimar TRUE 8 logreg mimar TRUE 9 polyreg mimar TRUE 10 rf wrapped TRUE # 15 more rows ``` ::: ::: ## Evaluation When the true values are known (after amputation, or from a simulation), `evaluate()` computes recovery metrics comparing imputed to true values: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} diag <- evaluate(imp_pmm) diag$distribution # observed vs. imputed means, SDs, unique counts ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # basetable: 5 x 9 variable type missing observed_unique imputed_unique observed_mean 1 Sepal.Length numeric 33 33 28 5.837607 2 Sepal.Width numeric 39 22 19 3.075676 3 Petal.Length numeric 34 42 38 3.755172 4 Petal.Width numeric 34 21 21 1.252586 5 Species factor 31 3 3 NA imputed_mean observed_sd imputed_sd 1 5.987273 0.8377645 0.7791618 2 3.035385 0.4509014 0.4011957 3 3.770000 1.8037808 1.5557433 4 1.076471 0.7519784 0.7701759 5 NA NA NA ``` ::: ::: ## Completing and pooling Extract a single completed dataset or pool regression estimates across all `m` imputations using Rubin's rules: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} completed <- complete(imp_pmm, which = 1) head(completed) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # basetable: 6 x 5 Sepal.Length Sepal.Width Petal.Length Petal.Width Species 1 5.1 3.5 1.4 0.2 setosa 2 4.9 3.0 1.4 0.2 setosa 3 4.7 3.2 1.3 0.2 versicolor 4 4.6 3.1 1.5 0.2 setosa 5 5.1 3.6 1.4 0.5 setosa 6 5.4 3.3 1.7 0.4 setosa ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # fit a model on each completed dataset, then pool the coefficients completed_list <- lapply(seq_len(imp_pmm$m), function(k) complete(imp_pmm, which = k)) fits <- lapply(completed_list, function(d) lm(Sepal.Length ~ Sepal.Width + Petal.Length + Petal.Width, data = d)) betas <- lapply(fits, coef) vars <- lapply(fits, function(f) diag(vcov(f))) pool(betas, variance = vars) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` mimar pooled results # basetable: 4 x 14 term estimate std.error statistic df p.value conf.low 1 (Intercept) 2.1204880 0.23942658 8.856527 Inf 8.254583e-19 1.6512205 2 Sepal.Width 0.5861945 0.06375298 9.194779 Inf 3.757668e-20 0.4612410 3 Petal.Length 0.7034397 0.05719104 12.299822 Inf 9.077385e-35 0.5913473 4 Petal.Width -0.5639728 0.12879778 -4.378746 Inf 1.193641e-05 -0.8164118 conf.high m within_variance between_variance total_variance 1 2.5897555 5 0.057325087 0 0.057325087 2 0.7111480 5 0.004064442 0 0.004064442 3 0.8155320 5 0.003270815 0 0.003270815 4 -0.3115338 5 0.016588867 0 0.016588867 relative_increase_variance rule 1 0 rubin 2 0 rubin 3 0 rubin 4 0 rubin ``` ::: ::: ## When to use mimar `mimar` is designed for: - **Simulation studies**: amputate, impute, evaluate recovery under controlled conditions - **Applied health research**: handle missing covariates or outcomes before regression or survival analysis - **ML-driven imputation**: when the imputation model is complex enough to warrant a tree ensemble or gradient booster ## Links - GitHub: [github.com/ielbadisy/mimar](https://github.com/ielbadisy/mimar)
